title: Teaching Gemini to Speak YouTube: Adapting LLMs for Video Recommendations to 2B+DAU - Devansh Tandon

summary:
Devansh argues recommendations will be a bigger consumer LLM application than search, though it's underhyped because it's transparent to users. YouTube's recommendation problem involves learning a function from user context (demographics, last 100 videos, engagement, subscriptions, comments) to video recommendations. The LRM system starts with base Gemini checkpoints, adapts them for YouTube-specific understanding, then aligns for retrieval and ranking tasks across major surfaces.

The first critical step is SemanticID: extracting video features (title, description, transcript, audio, video frames sampled from engagement hotspots) into multi-dimensional embeddings, quantized via RQVAE to assign each video semantically meaningful tokens forming a hierarchy (e.g., music→sports→volleyball). This replaces hash-based tokenization and creates atomic units for a new YouTube language. SemanticID training is entirely unsupervised—concepts like sports vs entertainment emerge organically. Video information is compressed into 8 tokens.

Continued pre-training teaches the model in two stages: linking text and SemanticIDs (e.g., prompting with a SID to predict titles or creators), then understanding watch sequences by masking videos and predicting them from engagement data. This produces a bilingual LLM reasoning across English and YouTube video space. A key challenge is catastrophic forgetting—overtraining on SemanticID examples causes the model to forget English; mixture of experts is being explored to retain text capability in some experts while others focus on SemanticIDs.

Generative retrieval constructs prompts with user demographics, context video, and watch history to decode recommendations as SIDs. LRM excels at hard recommendation tasks and cold-start users. SemanticID enables warm-starting into a semantically meaningful space, improving performance for fresh and tail content. Serving costs were prohibitive (95%+ savings needed); solutions include offline inference tables for head videos. Only videos are tokenized—not users; user tokenization remains a research direction. Scale requires smaller checkpoints (Flash and below) for latency at billions of DAU.

The 3-step recipe for adapting LLMs to any domain: (1) tokenize content into domain-specific atomic tokens, (2) adapt the LLM bilingually linking English and domain language, (3) prompt with personalized user info for generative recommendations. Future directions include interactive recommendations where users steer via natural language, explainable recommendations, blurring of search and recommendation lines, and eventually generating personalized content rather than just recommending it.

sections.title: Introduction: Recommendations vs Search
sections.summary: Devansh introduces recommendations as a bigger, underhyped LLM application compared to search. YouTube recommendations drive majority of watch time across home, watch next, shorts, and personalized search. The recommendation problem is framed as learning a function from user context to video recommendations.

sections.title: LRM: Adapting Gemini for YouTube
sections.summary: Introduces LRM (Large Recommender Model), starting with base Gemini checkpoint, adapting it for YouTube to create a unified checkpoint, then aligning for retrieval and ranking. Launched in production for retrieval; experimenting on ranking side.

sections.title: SemanticID: Tokenizing Videos
sections.summary: Explains SemanticID: extracting video features (title, description, transcript, audio, video frames) into multi-dimensional embeddings, quantized via RQVAE to assign each video tokens. Creates semantically meaningful hierarchy replacing hash-based tokenization. Paper presented at RecSys.

sections.title: Continued Pre-training: Linking Text and YouTube
sections.summary: Describes two-stage continued pre-training: linking text and SemanticIDs (predicting titles/creators from SIDs) and understanding watch sequences via masked video prediction. Model learns to reason across English and YouTube video space.

sections.title: Generative Retrieval and Serving Challenges
sections.summary: Covers generative retrieval constructing prompts with user demographics, context, and watch history to decode recommendations as SIDs. LRM excels at hard tasks and cold-start users but serving costs required 95%+ savings. Offline recommendation tables for head videos as cost workaround.

sections.title: YouTube-Specific Challenges
sections.summary: Contrasts YouTube challenges with traditional LLM training: 20B+ videos vs ~100K English words, freshness requirements (Taylor Swift video must recommend within minutes), and continuous pre-training on order of days/hours vs 3-6 months for Gemini.

sections.title: Scale, Recipe Summary, and Future Directions
sections.summary: Addresses scale: Gemini Pro cannot serve billions of DAU; YouTube uses smaller checkpoints like Flash and below for latency. Summarizes 3-step LLM+RecSys recipe: tokenize content, adapt LLM bilingually linking English and domain language, prompt with personalized user info. Future directions: interactive natural-language-steerable recommendations, explainable recommendations, blurring search/recommendation lines, and eventually generating personalized content rather than just recommending it.

sections.title: Q&A: Forgetting, Cold-Start, Frames, Pre-training, and Metrics
sections.summary: Q&A covers: (1) Catastrophic forgetting—overtraining on SemanticID causes English forgetting; mixture of experts explored to retain text in some experts. (2) SemanticID training is unsupervised; warm-starting in semantic space improves fresh/tail content performance. (3) Video frames sampled from engagement hotspots, compressed into 8 tokens; hard to know what specific visual details are captured. (4) Only videos tokenized, not users; focused on watch sequences not search queries; user tokenization is future research. (5) Cannot share metrics but describes LRM as the biggest improvement to recommendation quality in the last few years.

SemanticID hierarchy example: first token represents topics like music/gaming/sports, narrowing to volleyball, with shared prefix tokens for related videos
